paragraphs: The President is "to nominate, and, by and with the advice and consent of the Senate, to appoint ambassadors, other public ministers and consuls, judges of the Supreme Court, and all other officers of the United States whose appointments are not otherwise provided for in the Constitution. But the Congress may by law vest the appointment of such inferior officers as they think proper, in the President alone, or in the courts of law, or in the heads of departments. The President shall have power to fill up all vacancies which may happen during the recess of the Senate, by granting commissions which shall expire at the end of their next session."

I observed in an earlier paper that "the true test of a good government is its aptitude and tendency to produce a good administration." If that observation is just, then the method of appointing the officers of the United States set out in the clauses above must, once examined, be admitted to deserve particular praise. It is hard to imagine a plan better designed than this one to promote a sound choice of men to fill the offices of the Union, and it needs no proof that the character of the Union's administration must depend essentially on this point.

Everyone will agree that the power of appointment, in ordinary cases, ought to take one of three forms. It ought to be placed either in a single man, or in a select assembly of moderate size, or in a single man acting with the concurrence of such an assembly. That the people at large should exercise it will readily be admitted to be impractical, if only because, setting aside every other consideration, it would leave them little time for anything else. So when I speak of an assembly or body of men in the reasoning that follows, it must be understood to mean a select body or assembly of the kind just described. The people as a whole, because of their numbers and their scattered situation, cannot be guided in their movements by that systematic spirit of cabal and intrigue which will be urged as the chief objection to placing the power in question in a body of men.

Those who have thought about this subject themselves, or who have attended to the observations made elsewhere in these papers on the appointment of the President, will, I presume, agree that there would always be a strong probability of the office being filled by a man of at least respectable abilities. Taking this as given, I go on to lay down a rule: one man of discernment is better suited to analyze and judge the particular qualities fitted to particular offices than a body of men of equal, or perhaps even greater, discernment.

The sole and undivided responsibility of one man will naturally produce a livelier sense of duty and a more exact regard for reputation. For that reason he will feel himself under stronger obligations, and will have more reason to investigate carefully the qualities needed in the positions to be filled and to prefer, impartially, the persons with the fairest claims to them. He will have fewer personal attachments to gratify than a body of men, each of whom may be supposed to have as many, and so he will be that much less liable to be misled by feelings of friendship and affection. A single well-directed man, with a single understanding, cannot be distracted and twisted by that diversity of views, feelings, and interests which frequently distracts and twists the resolutions of a collective body. Nothing so readily stirs the passions of mankind as personal considerations, whether they concern ourselves or others who are to be the objects of our choice or preference. Hence, whenever an assembly of men exercises the power of appointing to offices, we must expect a full display of all the private and party likings and dislikes, biases and antipathies, attachments and animosities, felt by those who make up the assembly. A choice made under such circumstances will naturally be the result either of a victory won by one party over the other or of a compromise between the parties. In either case, the real merit of the candidate will too often be lost from sight. In the first case, the qualifications best suited to unite the votes of the party will be weighed more heavily than those that fit the person for the position. In the second, the coalition will commonly turn on some self-interested exchange: "Give us the man we wish for this office, and you shall have the one you wish for that." This will be the usual condition of the bargain. And it will rarely happen that the advancement of the public service is the primary object either of party victories or of party negotiations.

The truth of the principles advanced here seems to have been felt by the most intelligent of those who have found fault with the provision the Convention has made on this point. They contend that the President alone ought to have been authorized to make the appointments under the federal government. But it is easy to show that every advantage to be expected from such an arrangement would, in substance, come from the power of nomination that is proposed to be given him, while several disadvantages that might accompany the absolute power of appointment in the hands of that officer would be avoided. In the act of nomination his judgment alone would be exercised. Since it would be his sole duty to point out the man who, with the approval of the Senate, should fill an office, his responsibility would be as complete as if he were to make the final appointment. From this point of view there can be no difference between nominating and appointing. The same motives that would lead him to do his duty properly in one case would exist in the other. And since no man could be appointed except on his prior nomination, every man who might be appointed would in fact be his choice.

But might not his nomination be overruled? I grant that it might, yet this could only make room for another nomination by himself. The person finally appointed must be the object of his preference, though perhaps not his first preference. It is also not very probable that his nominations would often be overruled. The Senate could not be tempted, by a preference for someone else, to reject the person proposed, because they could not be sure that the person they wished for would be brought forward by a second nomination or by any later one. They could not even be certain that a future nomination would present a candidate in any degree more acceptable to them. And since their refusal might cast a kind of stigma on the person rejected, and might look like a reflection on the judgment of the chief executive, it is not likely that they would often withhold their approval unless there were special and strong reasons for doing so.

To what purpose, then, require the cooperation of the Senate? I answer that the necessity of their concurrence would have a powerful, though generally silent, effect. It would be an excellent check on a spirit of favoritism in the President, and would do much to prevent the appointment of unfit persons out of State prejudice, family connection, personal attachment, or a view to popularity. In addition, it would be an effective source of stability in the administration.

It is easy to see that a man who had the sole disposal of offices would be governed much more by his private inclinations and interests than when he was required to submit the propriety of his choice to the discussion and decision of a different and independent body, and that body an entire branch of the legislature. The possibility of rejection would be a strong motive to care in making proposals. The danger to his own reputation, and, in the case of an elected chief executive, to his political existence, from displaying a spirit of favoritism or an unbecoming pursuit of popularity before a body whose opinion would carry great weight in forming the public's, could not fail to work as a barrier against both. He would be both ashamed and afraid to bring forward, for the most distinguished or lucrative positions, candidates whose only merit was coming from the same State he himself belonged to, or being in some way personally allied to him, or having the necessary insignificance and pliancy to make them the servile instruments of his pleasure.

It has been objected to this reasoning that the President, through the influence of the power of nomination, may secure the compliance of the Senate with his views. To suppose universal venality in human nature is hardly less an error in political reasoning than to suppose universal rectitude. The institution of delegated power implies that there is a portion of virtue and honor among mankind that may be a reasonable foundation for confidence, and experience bears out the theory. It has been found to exist in the most corrupt periods of the most corrupt governments. The venality of the British House of Commons has long been a topic of accusation against that body, in its own country as well as in this one, and it cannot be doubted that the charge is, to a considerable extent, well founded. But it is just as little to be doubted that a large proportion of that body always consists of independent and public-spirited men who carry real weight in the councils of the nation. Hence it is (the present reign not excepted) that the sense of that body is often seen to control the inclinations of the monarch, with regard both to men and to measures. So although it might be allowable to suppose that the Executive might occasionally influence some individuals in the Senate, the supposition that he could in general buy the integrity of the whole body would be forced and improbable. A man disposed to view human nature as it is, neither flattering its virtues nor exaggerating its vices, will see sufficient ground for confidence in the honesty of the Senate. He will rest satisfied not only that it will be impracticable for the Executive to corrupt or seduce a majority of its members, but also that the necessity of its cooperation in the business of appointments will be a considerable and beneficial restraint on the conduct of that officer. Nor is the integrity of the Senate the only thing we can rely on. The Constitution has provided some important guards against the danger of executive influence on the legislative body. It declares that "No senator or representative shall during the time for which he was elected, be appointed to any civil office under the United States, which shall have been created, or the emoluments whereof shall have been increased, during such time; and no person, holding any office under the United States, shall be a member of either house during his continuance in office."
